messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For nearly twenty years, Daniel had made his living high above the street, laying shingles and patching roofs across suburban neighborhoods outside Boston. He was 43, married, practical, and used to thinking of himself as the man who kept working no matter the weather. That image of himself fractured the day he was downtown delivering materials near a transit station when an explosion tore through the block. He remembered the flash first and then the heat, a violent burst of air that seemed to punch through him. In the smoke and confusion, his chest slammed with terror so hard he thought his heart might give out. There was a scorched, chemical smell mixed with burning, and for a few moments he was convinced the whole street was on fire. He got clear physically, but what stayed with him was the sense that danger could erupt without warning and that his own body had become part of the alarm.

In the weeks afterward, Daniel noticed that certain sensations pulled him straight back toward that day. If he was climbing a ladder at work and his heart started pounding from exertion, he would suddenly go rigid, as if that familiar racing in his chest meant something catastrophic was about to happen. The smell of burnt material on a torch-down roofing job, or even a faint smoky odor drifting from a neighbor’s grill, could stop him mid-motion. In those moments the memory did not come back as a story he could tell. It hit him all at once, with such force that he had to shut it down. He would feel a sharp ache in the same parts of his body that had hurt after the blast, and when his wife asked what had just happened, he would say he knew exactly what he had seen but could not get the words out.

Because those moments felt unbearable, Daniel began organizing his days around not letting his mind settle. He kept the radio on in the truck, took extra jobs, scrolled on his phone during breaks, and stayed busy at home fixing things that did not really need fixing. When burnt or smoky smells caught him off guard on a roof, he would immediately redirect himself into measurements, tools, anything concrete that could pull him away from what was beginning to surface. He also stopped watching news coverage, action films, or anything about bombings or attacks. He told himself there was no point in filling his head with more of the same; privately, he knew that even brief reminders could set off the flood he was trying to outrun.

His body, meanwhile, never seemed to stand down. Daniel moved through the world braced and watchful, scanning rooftops, traffic, crowds, and sudden noises with a level of alertness that exhausted him. He sat in restaurants facing the door. On jobs in the city he tracked sirens and backfiring engines before anyone else seemed to notice them. This constant readiness made the trauma memory feel close to the surface. When he was already wound tight, it took very little for an image or bodily flash of the explosion to break through, and once it did, he was overwhelmed too quickly to stay with it for long.

Over time the memory itself became another trigger. He learned that even the beginning of it—the first whiff of smoke in his mind, the first bodily echo of pain, the first sense of his heart surging—could set off the same urgent alarm as something happening in front of him. That left him more determined to distract himself the instant anything related to the attack appeared. The more he cut away from it, the less able he felt to describe what had happened, and the more frightening it seemed whenever it forced its way back in. At work, this had started to cost him. On one recent roofing job, the odor from heated tar made him step away so abruptly that his coworker asked if he was sick. Daniel shrugged it off, but afterward he avoided that part of the job and stayed on edge for the rest of the day, embarrassed and irritated that his body had reacted before he could think.

At home, his wife had begun to notice that he was never really at rest. Even in the evenings he kept himself occupied, flipping channels until he landed on something harmless, leaving the room if a report about an attack came on, going out to the garage rather than sitting still. He did not tell her that what frightened him most was how quickly nothing could become something: a pounding heartbeat, a burnt smell, a flicker of memory, and suddenly he was back in danger. He finally came for help after a recent incident on a roof when his heart started racing from the climb and he froze, certain for a few seconds that another attack was unfolding. What he wants is simple enough to say, even if the rest is not: to work without feeling ambushed by his own body, and to be able to come home without carrying the blast with him.
